idiom_name: one table plus one mapper per concrete class, shared key source, union reader for hierarchy-wide access
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: give every concrete class its own table whose columns are that class's full persistent state (inherited members repeated), and one mapper per concrete class that reads and writes only its own table - no table for abstract classes, no discriminator column. Because no table owns the hierarchy's keys, generate identity from one shared source (sequence, GUID/UUID generator or explicitly seeded ranges) so keys stay unique when the tables are read together. Hierarchy-wide reads are assembled from a UNION ALL of the concrete tables, padding the columns that do not apply with NULL and synthesizing a type tag; make that union one named view or helper instead of repeating it in every query. Add back explicitly what the mapping removes: a key registry table if cross-type uniqueness or cross-type references are needed.
pitfalls: Skipping the shared key source and letting each table generate its own keys produces collisions as soon as the hierarchy is read as a whole.
Letting the duplicated base columns drift (different type, length or nullability per table) breaks the union at runtime and silently loses constraints.
Writing the union by hand in every query instead of in one view or helper spreads the NULL-padding contract across the codebase.
Pointing a foreign key at 'the base class' when no table holds all instances: the database cannot enforce such a reference.

Wrong move: pair TABLE_PER_CLASS with IDENTITY or AUTO id generation -> failure: JPA/Hibernate cannot guarantee unique keys across the per-table generators, so key generation fails or collides -> instead: use a shared sequence, a TABLE generator, or client-generated GUIDs.

Wrong move: model roles that instances change or share (a customer becomes an employee) on concrete tables -> failure: the move means copying the row to another table under a new key, and entities in two roles have no single home for their shared columns -> instead: use class table inheritance or replace the hierarchy with role rows.

Wrong move: rely on the provider to make TABLE_PER_CLASS portable -> failure: the strategy is optional in the JPA spec and some providers or tooling do not implement or model it, so the schema breaks on migration -> instead: verify provider support (and polymorphic-query behavior) before committing, or standardize on SINGLE_TABLE/JOINED.
